title: Assignment 05 Summary
text:
Overall purpose: Learn how to find, download, verify, and evaluate government documents for research using both a website and an API.
Step 0 — Set up access: Obtain a GovInfo API key and store it securely so R can access the API without exposing the key publicly.
Step 1 — Find the relevant documents: Search manually for Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings, sort newest first, and export a reference list.
Step 2 — Understand the API: Learn how to request collections, search results, document metadata, download links, and additional pages through R.
Step 3 — Collect and verify: Download ten hearings through both methods and compare their identifiers and order. Save logs showing download success. We verified the same ten hearing records, but did not compare the PDFs’ internal content.
Step 4 — Evaluate research usability: Explain the difficulties encountered and what text extraction, cleaning, or OCR might be needed to turn the documents into a table or text corpus. Consider how metadata and alternative formats could improve the process.
Step 5 — Document and share: Publish the code, report, and download log on your assignment webpage so the teaching assistant can review your process and results, while keeping the PDFs and API key out of the public repository.

Part 1: Practice scraping Books to Scrape
Turning information displayed on five webpages into one structured dataframe. Each row represents one book listing.

Part 1(a): Run the sample against the practice website

Books to Scrape is designed for scraping practice.
Its static HTML lets us practice extracting information without needing JavaScript tools.
We first read page 1 and inspect the extracted results before repeating the process across more pages.



Part 1(b): Extract titles, prices, and ratings from five pages

We extract each book’s title, price, and star rating.
We convert the price text into a numeric variable called price_gbp.
We repeat the extraction for pages 2–5 and reuse the page 1 results.
We combine the five page-level dataframes into books_all.
The expected result is 100 book listings, with 20 listings from each page.
The additional page column records where each listing came from.

library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)


## ---- 1. The sandbox: books.toscrape.com ------------------------------------
## Built and published for scraping practice. 1,000 books, 50 pages, no
## JavaScript. Learn the verbs here before you point them at anyone's server.

# Read the first page of book listings
books_pg <- read_html(
  "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-1.html"
)

books <- tibble(
  title  = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |> html_attr("title"),
  price  = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod p.price_color") |> html_text2(),
  rating = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod p.star-rating") |>
             html_attr("class") |> str_remove("star-rating ")
) |>
  mutate(price_gbp = parse_number(price))

Part 2: Scrape and clean Wikipedia tables
Extracting tables from a real website, adapting the program to another table, and cleaning the results into usable dataframes.

Part 2(a): Scrape the foreign-exchange reserves table

We checked the page’s robots rules before fetching it.
We inspected the candidate tables and extracted the reserves table.
We identified the including-gold amount column: foreign_exchange_reserves.
Its unit is US$ millions.
We retained the country, reserves amount, and reporting date.



Part 2(b): Scrape a different table and explain what changed

We changed the target to Wikipedia’s countries-and-dependencies population table.
The country column changed from country_as_recognized_by_the_un to location.
The amount column changed from foreign_exchange_reserves to population.
The reporting-date column changed from last_reporteddate to date.
Therefore, the column-selection code needed changing.
The reserves table contained two additional header rows that needed removal.
Both tables used day–month–year dates, so the same date-conversion function worked for both.

What broke and why: Column-specific code cannot automatically transfer between tables with different names. The placeholder errors we encountered were caused by unreplaced example names; they were not evidence that Wikipedia had changed its page.


Part 2(c): Clean the dataframes

Standardized column names.
Removed bracketed footnotes, thin spaces, nonbreaking spaces, and extra whitespace.
Removed unnecessary columns.
Removed repeated country headers and any Total or World rows.
Converted reserve amounts and population counts into numbers.
Converted reporting dates into R dates.
Preserved the original amount and date text to check conversions.
Added checks to identify missing or unsuccessfully converted values.

Obtaining reserves through a structured data interface and comparing them with the scraped Wikipedia figures.

Part 3(a): Fetch World Bank reserves

We used the WDI package to request indicator FI.RES.TOTL.CD, total reserves including gold in current US dollars.

Part 3: Download the data and calculate the poverty rate

This chunk downloads the 2024 ACS estimates, margins of error, and geographic boundaries for Texas counties. The E suffix identifies an estimate, while the M suffix identifies its margin of error. It then calculates the poverty rate and propagates the uncertainty using moe_prop().

# Download the selected ACS variables and Texas county geometry
# Wide output produces one row per county with separate estimate and MOE columns
acs_wide <- get_acs(
    geography = geo_level,  # Use counties as the geographic unit
    variables = my_vars,    # Download the three selected ACS variables
    state = state_abbr,     # Limit the data to Texas
    year = year_acs,        # Use the 2024 ACS
    survey = survey,        # Use the ACS 5-year estimates
    geometry = TRUE,        # Retain county boundaries for mapping
    output = "wide"         # Produce one row for each county
)

# Derive the poverty rate and carry its margin of error through
acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
    mutate(
        pov_rate = povE / povdenE, # Divide poverty count by its denominator
        pov_moe = moe_prop(        # Calculate the MOE for the poverty rate
            povE,                  # Poverty-count estimate
            povdenE,               # Poverty-denominator estimate
            povM,                  # MOE for the poverty-count estimate
            povdenM                # MOE for the denominator estimate
        )
    )

text:
4(a) Map Interpretation
The map shows substantial variation in median household income across Texas counties. Higher-income counties appear primarily around major metropolitan areas, especially the Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin, and Houston regions. Many counties in South Texas, along the Rio Grande border, and in parts of West Texas have lower median household incomes. Overall, the pattern suggests that counties near large urban economies tend to have higher household incomes than many rural and border counties.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(b) Table Interpretation
The highest estimated poverty rate is in Dimmit County at approximately 41.1%, followed by Zapata County at 38.4% and Zavala County at 33.9%. Many counties in the highest-poverty group are located in South Texas or near the Texas–Mexico border. In contrast, Rockwall County has the lowest estimated poverty rate at approximately 4.0%, followed by Sterling County at 4.3% and Sutton County at 4.5%. The margins of error vary substantially across counties, meaning the estimated ordering should be interpreted cautiously, particularly for counties with relatively large margins of error.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(c) Uncertainty Check
Dimmit County and Zapata County provide one clear example of overlapping confidence intervals.

Dimmit County: estimated poverty rate = 41.1%, MOE = 8.9 percentage points, interval = 32.2%–50.0%.
Zapata County: estimated poverty rate = 38.4%, MOE = 6.0 percentage points, interval = 32.4%–44.4%.

The two intervals overlap substantially. Therefore, although Dimmit County is ranked above Zapata County based on the point estimates, the data do not provide strong evidence that Dimmit County’s true poverty rate is higher. Sampling uncertainty could reverse or eliminate the apparent difference. The ranking should consequently be treated as descriptive rather than as a definitive ordering of the counties.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(d) Methods Note
This analysis uses 2024 American Community Survey five-year estimates for Texas counties. Counties were selected because they provide meaningful geographic comparisons while remaining readable on a statewide map. Median household income (B19013_001) was mapped to show the geographic distribution of economic resources. Poverty was measured using the population below the poverty level (B17001_002) divided by the population for whom poverty status was determined (B17001_001). Using a rate instead of a raw count prevents counties with larger populations from appearing more disadvantaged simply because they contain more residents. I retained the ACS margins of error and used moe_prop() to propagate uncertainty into the calculated poverty rate. The margins of error show that some county estimates are much less precise than others. Several confidence intervals overlap, so small differences between counties should not be interpreted as definitive differences in their true poverty rates. Consequently, the top-and-bottom rankings are descriptive and should be interpreted cautiously.

The identical results may mean that Google returned the same sample or a cached version of the data during the short interval between my calls. A query repeated later could still produce different values. Therefore, every finding reported from Google Trends should be treated as an estimate of relative search interest rather than an exact count. Researchers should record the complete query parameters and retrieval time, save the original data, and repeat important queries to test whether their substantive conclusions remain stable. I created this website using RStudio and Quarto. The website provides a professional, organized platform where visitors can learn about my academic background, research interests, teaching activities, curriculum vitae, and course assignments.
I used the Cosmo theme because it offers a clean, professional appearance. The design is simple and easy to read, allowing visitors to focus on the website’s content. I also used a custom CSS file to support the overall appearance and formatting of the website.

The Resume link provides direct access to my updated résumé. I included it in the main navigation bar so that visitors can easily view my academic and professional qualifications.

## EPPS 6302
## Assignment 2 - Part A.4(a)
## Website versus gtrendsR: Past five years

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 1. Pull the five-year data using gtrendsR
## ---------------------------------------------------------

r_pull <- gtrends(
  keyword = c("Trump", "Kamala Harris", "Election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

r_df <- r_pull$interest_over_time

# Save the original R data
write_csv(
  r_df,
  "part4a_r_raw.csv"
)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 2. Read the five-year website CSV
## ---------------------------------------------------------

website_df <- read_csv(
  "time_series_US_20210916-1050_20260916-1050_Trump_Kamala Harris_Election_5 year_Gtrend web data.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Remove spaces from column names
names(website_df) <- trimws(names(website_df))

# Rename the first column
names(website_df)[1] <- "date"

View(website_df)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 3. Convert website data from wide to long format
## ---------------------------------------------------------

website_long <- website_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "keyword",
    values_to = "website_hits"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = format(date, "%Y-%m"),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    website_hits = as.numeric(website_hits)
  )

View(website_long)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 4. Prepare the R data
## ---------------------------------------------------------

r_long <- r_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = format(date, "%Y-%m"),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    
    # Replace "<1" with 0.5 so that it is not converted to NA
    r_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

View(r_long)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 5. Convert both datasets to monthly observations
## ---------------------------------------------------------

# The website data are already monthly, but this confirms
# that there is one value per term per month.

website_monthly <- website_long %>%
  group_by(month, keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    website_hits = mean(website_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Average the weekly R observations within each month.

r_monthly <- r_long %>%
  group_by(month, keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    r_hits = mean(r_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 6. Match the website and R observations
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison <- inner_join(
  website_monthly,
  r_monthly,
  by = c("month", "keyword")
) %>%
  mutate(
    difference = r_hits - website_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference),
    
    direction = case_when(
      difference > 0 ~ "R higher",
      difference < 0 ~ "Website higher",
      TRUE ~ "Identical"
    )
  )

View(comparison)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 7. Calculate the differences
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison_summary <- comparison %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    matched_months = n(),
    
    identical_values =
      sum(difference == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    different_values =
      sum(difference != 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_website_value =
      mean(website_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_R_value =
      mean(r_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_difference =
      mean(difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_absolute_difference =
      mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    maximum_absolute_difference =
      max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    general_direction = case_when(
      mean_difference > 0 ~ "R generally higher",
      mean_difference < 0 ~ "Website generally higher",
      TRUE ~ "Same average"
    ),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

comparison_summary


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 8. Confirm that all three terms were matched
## ---------------------------------------------------------

table(comparison$keyword)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 9. Plot the two methods
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison_plot_data <- comparison %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01"))
  ) %>%
  select(
    date,
    keyword,
    website_hits,
    r_hits
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(website_hits, r_hits),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "hits"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    method = recode(
      method,
      website_hits = "Google Trends website",
      r_hits = "gtrendsR"
    )
  )

part4a_plot <- ggplot(
  comparison_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = hits,
    color = method
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ keyword,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Google Trends Website and gtrendsR Comparison",
    subtitle = "United States, Web Search, Past Five Years",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Relative search interest",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

part4a_plot


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 10. Save the outputs
## ---------------------------------------------------------

write_csv(
  website_monthly,
  "part4a_website_monthly.csv"
)

write_csv(
  r_monthly,
  "part4a_r_monthly.csv"
)

write_csv(
  comparison,
  "part4a_comparison.csv"
)

write_csv(
  comparison_summary,
  "part4a_comparison_summary.csv"
)

ggsave(
  filename = "part4a_comparison_plot.png",
  plot = part4a_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 11. Display the saved files
## ---------------------------------------------------------

list.files(
  pattern = "^part4a_",
  full.names = TRUE
)


## 4 Part c)
pull_1 <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

pull_1_df <- pull_1$interest_over_time

write_csv(
  pull_1_df,
  "part4c_pull_1.csv"
)



## Waiting for 2 minutes before running the second block of code

pull_2 <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

pull_2_df <- pull_2$interest_over_time

write_csv(
  pull_2_df,
  "part4c_pull_2.csv"
)


## Comparing the two pulled data 2 minutes apart
pull_1_clean <- pull_1_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    pull_1_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

pull_2_clean <- pull_2_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    pull_2_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

repeated_comparison <- inner_join(
  pull_1_clean,
  pull_2_clean,
  by = c("date", "keyword")
) %>%
  mutate(
    difference = pull_2_hits - pull_1_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  )

View(repeated_comparison)


## Comparison Summary

repeated_summary <- repeated_comparison %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    matched_observations = n(),
    identical_values =
      sum(difference == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    different_values =
      sum(difference != 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_difference =
      mean(difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_absolute_difference =
      mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum_absolute_difference =
      max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

repeated_summary


write_csv(
  repeated_comparison,
  "part4c_repeated_comparison.csv"
)

write_csv(
  repeated_summary,
  "part4c_repeated_summary.csv"
)

text:
Part 4: Data Acquisition Plan
Research purpose

We will examine whether burglary/breaking and entering, destruction/damage/vandalism of property, motor vehicle theft, and robbery co-locate with recorded drug/narcotic violations and documented homeless encampments in Downtown Dallas and the Harry Hines corridor. We will investigate whether observed patterns also reflect differences in police activity; spatial association alone will not establish causation.

(a) Sources and reasons for choosing them

We will retain three Dallas OpenData datasets: Police Incidents (qv6i-rri7), Police Arrests (sdr7-6v3j), and Dallas Police Active Calls (9fxf-t2tr). They provide complementary information about recorded offenses, arrests, and calls being handled.
Police Incidents will be the main dataset because it contains NIBRS_Crime_Category, which identifies the selected offenses. Arrests and calls will provide additional context about police activity, subject to their coverage and available fields.
We have requested GIS shapefiles for homeless encampments and sexually oriented businesses. We will obtain or define study-area boundaries and check each layer’s observation dates and coordinate system.
We will verify IncidentNum as a linkage field in each table. Because an incident may have multiple offenses, arrests, or call records, We will examine duplicates and summarize related records before joining to avoid inflating counts.

(b) Robots rules and Terms of Service

Before collection, We will check the portal’s robots.txt for the intended paths and review Dallas OpenData’s Terms of Use and dataset-specific licensing. We will record the results and the date checked.
Permission has not yet been verified. We will use only access methods permitted by the applicable rules and terms, follow any attribution requirements, and check restrictions attached to the requested GIS files. A robots check alone does not establish permission for every use.

(c) API availability and scraping justification

The supplied R script uses Socrata API endpoints to retrieve the three datasets as JSON. We will use the API or downloadable exports instead of scraping the displayed tables.
API queries allow filtering and pagination. We will adapt the script’s example filters—August 2020 and sector 640—to the agreed research period and geography; those example settings do not define my study areas.
We will confirm whether Active Calls retains historical records. If it only provides a changing current snapshot, I will request an archive or use it prospectively rather than treating it as a complete historical calls dataset.

(d) Volume, rate limiting, and caching

We will estimate record counts before downloading and retrieve only necessary fields and dates. Pagination will use stable ordering and an endpoint-supported batch size; the script’s 50,000-row setting will be tested.
We will make sequential requests, initially pause one second between batches, use an application token where appropriate, and increase waits after throttling responses. This pause is a proposed collection practice, not a verified portal limit.
We will cache dated raw downloads, metadata, query settings, and cleaned files. Analysis will use cached copies, with controlled refreshes instead of repeated downloads.

(e) Changes and detection

Collection may fail if field names, category labels, endpoints, date formats, coordinates, or identifier conventions change.
We will check required columns, exact offense labels, missing coordinates, date coverage, duplicate identifiers, record counts, and unmatched joins after each download. Unexpected changes will trigger review before analysis.
We will retain original snapshots and document corrections. Spatial and temporal aggregation will use consistent boundaries and periods, including the observation dates of encampment and business locations.

## Function to download PDFs

download_govfiles_pdf <- function(url, id) {
  tryCatch({
    destfile <- paste0(save_dir, "govfiles_", id, ".pdf")

    status <- download.file(
      url,
      destfile = destfile,
      mode = "wb"
    )

    if (status != 0) {
      stop("Download failed")
    }

    # Check that the downloaded file has a PDF header
    pdf_header <- readBin(destfile, what = "raw", n = 5)

    if (!identical(pdf_header, charToRaw("%PDF-"))) {
      stop("Downloaded file is not a PDF")
    }

    Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))

    return(paste("Successfully downloaded:", id))
  },
  error = function(e) {
    return(paste("Failed to download:", id))
  })
}

Step 4 : Report

Difficulties encountered
I downloaded the ten most recent Senate Committee on Foreign Relations hearings available through the refined GovInfo search, including subcommittee hearings, using both a website CSV export and API search results. Both methods successfully downloaded ten PDFs and returned the same ten hearings in the same order.
The initial phrase search also returned a hearing issued by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation because it mentioned Foreign Relations. I addressed this by restricting the search to the Senate chamber and the Foreign Relations committee. I also encountered an R error when combining API results because some fields contained nested lists of unequal lengths. Extracting simple fields before combining the records resolved this problem. Another error occurred when combining download logs before the CSV log object had been created; creating the missing log resolved it.


a. Usability of the documents as data
The PDFs provide source documents for analysis, but downloading them does not automatically produce an analysis-ready dataset. Their text must first be extracted and checked for completeness. Any scanned pages without usable embedded text would require optical character recognition (OCR). Headers, footers, page numbers, and formatting may also require cleaning, while tables and images may need separate processing.
To create a document-level table, I would use one row per hearing and include its package ID, title, date, committee, and document link. To create a text corpus, I would extract each hearing’s text, associate it with its package ID, and check the extraction against the original PDF. Analysis of individual statements would require additional work to identify speakers and separate their testimony.


b. Improvements to the process
I would use committee and chamber metadata filters from the beginning rather than relying only on a phrase search. I would also examine the available HTML or text versions before extracting text from PDFs, since these formats may simplify text processing. The PDFs would remain useful for checking the original layout, tables, and images.
Metadata can supply identifiers, titles, dates, committee information, and available download links without manually opening each hearing. I would preserve this metadata alongside the download log, record the query and sorting settings, and add retries for failed requests. If collecting more documents, I would use pagination to retrieve additional results.


c. What the API added
The API provided structured search results and document metadata that R could retrieve directly, reducing the manual exporting and page parsing required by website searches and scraping. It also supported repeatable requests with specified queries, sorting, and pagination, making the collection process easier to document and rerun.
